summary.text: Impulse is the change in an object's momentum, most often used for forces that act for a short time, as in impacts and collisions.
Like momentum it has a size and a direction, and its SI unit is the newton-second, dimensionally equal to kilogram metre per second.
A constant force acting for a time gives an impulse equal to force times time, and in rocketry impulse per unit of propellant gives a performance number called specific impulse.

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: The change in an object's momentum

facts.label: Vector?
facts.value: Yes, it has size and direction

facts.label: Rocketry term
facts.value: Total impulse means the same thing

facts.label: Specific impulse
facts.value: Impulse per unit mass of propellant

items.prompt: A kick changes a ball's momentum by 4 kg⋅m/s toward the goal. What is the impulse of the kick?

options.label: 8 N⋅s, double the change
4 N⋅s, pointing the way the momentum changed
4 N⋅s, with no direction
4 N⋅s, pointing back at the kicker

items.explain: Impulse is the momentum change, a vector, and N⋅s is equivalent to kg⋅m/s.

items.prompt: Why do game physics engines treat a collision's push as instant?

options.label: Real collisions take exactly zero time
Impulse exists only for one-second pushes
Instant changes need no force at all
It is not literally possible but simplifies ideal collisions

items.explain: The step change is not physically possible, yet it is a useful model for ideal collisions.

items.prompt: Two rocket engines give the same total push over a burn, but engine X burns half as much propellant. Which has the higher specific impulse?

options.label: Engine X, the one using less propellant
The one burning more propellant
Neither, since propellant is ignored
They match, since the totals are equal

items.explain: Specific impulse is impulse per unit of propellant, so the same impulse from less propellant scores higher.

items.prompt: A physicist says impulse and momentum share the same basic dimensions. Which pair of units shows it?

options.label: Joule and kilogram-metre
Newton-metre and kilogram-second
Newton-second and kilogram metre per second
Watt and kilogram metre per second

items.explain: The newton-second is the SI unit of impulse and is dimensionally equivalent to momentum's kg⋅m/s.

items.prompt: A puck slides into the rink edge and bounces straight back. Which way does the impulse on the puck point?

options.label: Toward the edge, the way it first travelled
Along the edge, sideways to both
It has no direction at all
Away from the edge, the way its motion changed

items.explain: Impulse is a vector pointing the way the momentum changed, here back out from the edge.

items.prompt: For which kind of force is it most natural to talk about impulse?

options.label: A push that lasts only a moment, like a hit
A steady pull that lasts for hours
A force that never changes direction
A force on an object that is not moving

items.explain: The term is most often used for forces acting over short time periods, as in impacts and collisions.
